=== CALL C0390 ===
Claire: Hello! Oh, hi, can you hear me okay?
Nicola: Yeah, I can hear you fine, love. Hiya. I'm Nicola. How are you doing?
Claire: I'm good, thanks. I'm Claire. Erm, a bit thrown by that puzzle at the start, if I'm honest. How about you?
Nicola: Oh God, the puzzle. I sort of stared at it for ages and then just guessed. Anyway, I'm alright, thanks. Bit stiff today, the weather's been doing my joints in, but I'm fine. Where are you, then?
Claire: Catford, South East London. And you?
Nicola: St Helens. Between Liverpool and Wigan, if you've not heard of it. I've got to say, I was looking at your photo earlier and I was dying to have a proper nosy at your bookshelf.
Claire: My bookshelf! Oh, it's a mess, honestly. It's mostly Scandi crime and whatever my book group's made me read. We're doing, erm, a Jon Fosse at the moment, which is sort of hard going.
Nicola: Oh, I tried one of his. Library e-book. It's all one long sentence, isn't it? I had to keep stopping. I'm more of a historical fiction person, and poetry. Carol Ann Duffy, Simon Armitage.
Claire: Oh, I love Armitage. Do you get through a lot?
Nicola: Loads. It's sort of all I can do some days, to be honest. I'm off work long-term with rheumatoid arthritis, so... I'm not being miserable about it, it's just how it is. The library app's my best friend. Except there's a waiting list on the one I want now, I'm about fortieth.
Claire: Fortieth! That's brutal. What did you do before, if you don't mind me asking?
Nicola: No, not at all. I was a care assistant in a residential home for years, then a school kitchen. I loved the care work, you know. Sitting with people, hearing the same story about their wedding for the fifth time. I miss that, do you know what I mean?
Claire: Yeah, I do, actually. That's kind of the bit of my job I like best.
Nicola: What do you do?
Claire: I'm a housing officer, for a housing association. I've got a patch of about three hundred flats across Lewisham and Greenwich, so it's sign-ups, home visits, rent arrears, neighbour disputes. A lot of it's paperwork, but the visits are where you actually find out what's going on with people. Some days it's lovely, and some days it's, erm, damp and mould and a family of five in a one-bed, and you come home and you can't switch off.
Nicola: Oh, that's funny, I rent off a housing association. Two-bed, me and the two kids.
Claire: Oh, really? Are they any good? You can be honest, I won't take it personally.
Nicola: They're alright, actually. They took six weeks to fix the back door once, but they put the grab rails in quick when I asked. I think it depends who you get, doesn't it? If you get someone who rings you back, that's half of it.
Claire: That's exactly it. I'm a bit obsessive about ringing people back. If I say Thursday, I ring Thursday.
Nicola: See, you'd be one of the good ones.
Claire: I try. What else fills your days, besides the reading?
Nicola: Birds, mainly. I've got a nest box out the back and the blue tits are back in it, I'm made up. And I do little watercolours when my hands let me. I start loads and finish about one in five.
Claire: That's better than my pottery. I make mugs that come out a weird colour and give them to people who are too polite to say anything.
Nicola: I'd have one! Are those the ones on your top shelf?
Claire: Yeah, those are the survivors. The green one was meant to be blue.
Nicola: Ah, it's character, that. My Ellie's the creative one in our house now, she's fifteen. She's been doing TikTok recipes, made us a Thai green curry for tea last week and it was actually lovely.
Claire: Oh, good on her. I keep trying to do Ottolenghi for dinner and it takes me about three hours.
Nicola: Ellie'd have a go at that. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry.
Claire: No, not at all, this is nice. I think we've probably not got long left, have we?
Nicola: No, it goes quick, doesn't it? It's been lovely talking to you, Claire.
Claire: You too. Good luck with the waiting list.

=== CALL C0391 ===
Darren: Hello, there we go. Can you hear me alright?
Rasa: Yes, hello. I can hear you. I'm Rasa.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from, then?
Rasa: Leyton, East London. And you?
Darren: Kesgrave, just outside Ipswich. Suffolk.
Rasa: Ah, okay. I don't know it, sorry. I know Ipswich only from the train board.
Darren: Ha, that's most people, to be fair. It's alright, it's quiet. So what do you do, Rasa?
Rasa: I work in a bakery in Walthamstow. Part-time, Saturday morning and one day in the week. Saturday is crazy, queue out the door from eight o'clock.
Darren: I bet. What, all the sausage rolls?
Rasa: Sausage rolls, yeah, and the bread. Everybody wants sourdough now. I bring home what is left at the end, so we never buy bread, that's good. And you? I guessed from your photo maybe builder or plumber.
Darren: Not far off. Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Installs, servicing, breakdowns. Got me own business, one van, been doing it about fourteen years.
Rasa: Oh, really? Then I need you. My boiler, every winter it stops. The pressure goes down, and the landlord takes like two weeks to send someone.
Darren: Yeah, that's a classic, that. Pressure dropping, you've probably got a little leak somewhere or the expansion vessel's gone. Landlord's probably just getting the cheapest bloke round to top it up, you know.
Rasa: Yes! Exactly. The man comes, he does something for five minutes and goes. And then three weeks later, again.
Darren: Sounds about right. It's mad busy in the winter anyway. Everyone's boiler packs up the first cold week. I was doing twelve-hour days in January.
Rasa: Twelve hours, every day? You must be knackered.
Darren: Yeah, the knees aren't what they were, to be fair. I'm hoping to take on an apprentice in a year or two, so I can do more of the quoting and less lying on kitchen floors.
Rasa: That makes sense. My husband is electrician, he says same thing about his back.
Darren: Oh, is he? Self-employed?
Rasa: No, he works for a company, maintenance for buildings. This week he is in Stratford on a job. He likes it, regular money, you know.
Darren: Yeah, there's a lot to be said for that. Being your own boss sounds good till the van breaks down. Mine's been playing up, sensor fault, had it in the garage last week. Are you from London originally?
Rasa: No, I'm from Lithuania, from Šiauliai. I came in 2006. So, nearly twenty years now.
Darren: Twenty years, blimey. Do you get back much?
Rasa: Every summer. Two, three weeks with my mum and my sister. We fly from Stansted, Ryanair. My daughter, she is twelve, she loves it there because grandma spoils her.
Darren: Course she does. Mine were the same with my mum. We usually do Spain or Turkey, all-inclusive, pool, bit of sun. Did Florida once with the kids, that was something.
Rasa: Florida, wow. That's expensive, no?
Darren: Erm, yeah, you don't want to know. Worth it, though. Lithuania, that's basketball, isn't it? I remember something about that.
Rasa: Yes! Basketball is like religion there. I don't really follow, but when Lithuania plays in big tournament, my husband watches and I have to watch too. That's it, really.
Darren: Ha, same as me with Ipswich and my wife. She just sits there on her phone.
Rasa: Yeah, same. I make dinner and I hear him shouting from the other room.
Darren: Sounds like ours on a Saturday. Right, I reckon we're nearly out of time.
Rasa: Yeah, it's fast. Nice to talk to you, Darren.
Darren: You too, Rasa. Get your landlord to sort that vessel out.

=== CALL C0392 ===
Megan: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
Claire: Yes, hi! I can hear you fine. I'm Claire.
Megan: I'm Megan. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous, I always think I'm doing these wrong.
Claire: Oh, I think we all are. That puzzle at the start threw me completely.
Megan: Oh my God, same. I read the instructions twice and still wasn't sure. Erm, where are you based?
Claire: Catford, South East London. You?
Megan: Stockton-on-Tees. Norton, technically, if that makes sense. North East, but not Newcastle.
Claire: Not Newcastle, noted. I won't say Geordie.
Megan: Thank you! People always do. So what do you do?
Claire: I'm a housing officer for a housing association. I look after about three hundred flats, so it's home visits, rent arrears, repairs, people falling out with their neighbours. Quite a lot of listening, really. What about you? I guessed nursing from your photo, I don't know why.
Megan: Close! I'm doing diagnostic radiography at Teesside, second year. So X-rays, basically, and then CT and things later. I've got placements at James Cook and North Tees, so it's sort of half uni, half hospital.
Claire: Oh, that's interesting. Do you like the hospital side?
Megan: I do, yeah. I get dead anxious before placements, like I can't sleep the night before sometimes, but once I'm there it's fine. I'm good with the older patients, they're usually nervous as well, so we're nervous together. My shifts start at half seven, so I'm up at six, and the parking at James Cook is shocking, honestly.
Claire: Hospital parking, that's universal, isn't it? Was it always radiography for you?
Megan: Erm, no, not really. I started Biomedical Science at eighteen and left after the first year, it felt a bit too abstract. Then I worked in a pharmacy for nearly three years. So I'm kind of a bit behind, if that makes sense.
Claire: Behind? I don't think that's behind at all. I did my housing qualification part-time in my thirties, and half the people on it were career changers. Working in a pharmacy probably makes you better at the patient bit, you know?
Megan: Yeah, that's what my mam says. And the paperwork. I'm quite fussy about request forms because of the pharmacy.
Claire: That's a good thing to be fussy about. I'm the same with case notes. Colleagues tease me, but then they come and ask me what they wrote.
Megan: Ha, yeah. Is your job quite stressful, then?
Claire: Erm, sometimes, yeah. Damp and mould cases, families squashed into one-beds. You do take some of it home. I swim in the mornings, which helps clear my head.
Megan: I do parkrun, when I'm not on placement. Preston Park, Saturday mornings. I'm on week five of my running plan as well.
Claire: Week five, that's good going. I gave up running, dodgy knee. Do you live near the hospital?
Megan: No, I'm at home with my mam and stepdad and my little brother. He's sixteen and eats everything in the fridge. My mam's done mince and dumplings for tea tonight, so I'll have to be quick.
Claire: Mince and dumplings, that sounds lovely. My husband works evenings so I mostly cook dinner for one.
Megan: Oh, that's a shame. Is that a lot of cooking for one person?
Claire: Too much, usually. I make Ottolenghi things that take three hours and then eat them for four days.
Megan: Sorry, I'm just thinking, I don't even know what Ottolenghi is. Is that a person?
Claire: It is, yes, a chef. Lots of pomegranate. You're not missing much on a Tuesday.
Megan: I'll stick with my chicken and rice in a tub, I think.
Claire: Honestly, that sounds very sensible. I think we're nearly out of time.
Megan: Oh, already? It's been really nice, thank you.
Claire: You too, Megan. Good luck with placement.

=== CALL C0393 ===
Nicola: Hiya! Can you hear me, love?
Rasa: Yes, I hear you. Hello, I'm Rasa.
Nicola: Nicola. Nice to meet you. How are you doing today?
Rasa: I'm okay, thank you. Bit tired. And you?
Nicola: Oh, same, I'm always a bit tired, don't worry. Where are you?
Rasa: Leyton, East London.
Nicola: I'm St Helens, up near Liverpool. I'll be honest, when I saw your photo I thought, she looks like a busy mum like me. Nice tidy kitchen, mind. Mine's a tip.
Rasa: Ha, it's tidy only for the photo. I thought same about you, tired mum. How many kids?
Nicola: Two. Ellie's fifteen and Jake's twelve. You?
Rasa: One. Emilija, she is twelve. Year 8.
Nicola: Same as Jake! Are they driving you mad yet? Jake's football boots already don't fit him, I only bought them in September.
Rasa: Yes, the shoes. And the school, always they want money for something. Now is some project, we have to buy another thing. Every week another thing.
Nicola: Oh, tell me about it. And everything's gone up. I do most of mine at Aldi and the reduced shelf, and even that's dear now.
Rasa: Lidl for me. Prices are crazy, yeah. Do you work?
Nicola: Not at the minute, no. I've got rheumatoid arthritis, so I've been off sick about four years. I used to be a carer in a residential home. Ellie does a lot of the shopping now, bless her, and some of the cooking. She did a Thai green curry from TikTok last week and it was actually lovely.
Rasa: Oh, that's nice she helps. Thai curry, it's spicy, no?
Nicola: A bit, yeah. Are you not a spice person?
Rasa: No, not really. I'm Lithuanian, we eat potatoes, potatoes, more potatoes. At weekend I made cepelinai, it takes all afternoon.
Nicola: What's cepelinai, then? Sorry, have I said that right?
Rasa: Yes, close. It's like big potato dumpling, with meat inside, and you put sour cream and bacon on top. Shape like a zeppelin, that's why the name. My daughter loves it, my husband loves it, I'm knackered after.
Nicola: Oh, that sounds right up my street. We do scouse when it's cold, which is sort of the same idea, meat and potato and you're full till next week.
Rasa: Scouse is what?
Nicola: It's a stew, lamb or beef with potatoes and carrots, cooked for ages. Liverpool thing. You have it with red cabbage and bread. Do you cook every night?
Rasa: Most nights, yes. I make dinner, if I'm tired then pasta. I work in bakery, so we always have bread, I bring home what's left.
Nicola: Free bread! I'd be made up with that. Do you go back to Lithuania much?
Rasa: Every summer, two or three weeks. My mum is there alone, so I worry a bit. We speak on video every Sunday.
Nicola: Ah, that's nice you do that. My mum died two years ago and I still go to ring her sometimes, do you know what I mean? So keep doing your Sundays.
Rasa: Yes. I'm sorry about your mum.
Nicola: Thank you, love. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry. I think we're nearly done.
Rasa: Yeah, it was nice to talk to you, Nicola.
Nicola: You too, Rasa. Enjoy your cepelinai.

=== CALL C0395 ===
Nicola: Hiya! Can you hear me alright, love?
Darren: Yeah, loud and clear. Hello. I'm Darren.
Nicola: Darren! Oh, that's funny. My husband's called Darren. Well, sort of ex-husband. We're separated, never got round to the divorce.
Darren: Ha, hopefully I'm not putting you off, then.
Nicola: No, no, he's alright, we get on fine. I'm Nicola, anyway. Where are you?
Darren: Kesgrave, near Ipswich. Suffolk. You?
Nicola: St Helens, between Liverpool and Wigan. I'll be honest, I looked at your photo and thought, he looks like my dad or one of my brothers. Just a normal bloke who knows what he's doing.

Nicola: Oh, bless you. What do you do, then?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Got my own business, one van, about fourteen years now.
Nicola: Ooh, I could do with you. Mine makes this horrible banging noise when the heating first comes on. The housing association sent someone and he said it was normal.
Darren: Banging? Could be air in the system, or a bit of sludge in the pipes. It's not dangerous usually, but it's not normal either. I'd get them back out, if I'm honest.

Nicola: Ah, I don't know about that. You're the one lying on kitchen floors.
Darren: Ha, true. I'm hoping to get an apprentice in, so I can do more quoting and less crawling about.
Nicola: That's sensible. My dad worked at the glassworks his whole life and his back was knackered by fifty. So you look after yourself.

Nicola: Ha, that'd be me. I'd have a book on my knee. How many kids have you got?

=== CALL C0396 ===
Megan: Hiya, can you hear me okay?
Nicola: Yeah, I can hear you, love. Hiya, I'm Nicola.
Megan: I'm Megan. Sorry, I always say that at the start, like the internet's going to go.
Nicola: Ah, you're fine. How are you doing? Have they worn you out yet?
Megan: A bit, yeah. I'm okay, though. Erm, I'm in Stockton, Norton really. Where are you?
Nicola: St Helens, up by Liverpool. I'll be honest, when I saw your photo I thought, she looks like me when I was starting out in care. Tired but capable.

Megan: Sorry, I meant it in a nice way! She's lovely. I do jigsaws with her most Sundays.

Nicola: Mostly, yeah. The ones I remember are the radiographers who don't rush you. When your hands are bad and someone's trying to get your fingers flat on the plate, and they just say, take your time, there's no hurry. That makes the whole day better, do you know what I mean?
Megan: Yeah. That's kind of what I worry about, getting it wrong with someone like that. I'm good with older patients, I think, but I check everything about five times.
Nicola: Better that than not checking. I did care work for years, and the ones who worried were always the good ones.

=== CALL C0397 ===
Claire: Hello, hi. Can you hear me?
Darren: Yeah, hello. I'm Darren.
Claire: Claire. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from?
Darren: Kesgrave, near Ipswich. You?
Claire: Catford, South East London. What do you do, Darren?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, heating. Self-employed, one van, about fourteen years.
Claire: Oh, I'll be honest, I guessed something like that. You reminded me of some of the contractors I work with.
Darren: Ha, is that good or bad?
Claire: Mostly good. Depends on the contractor. I'm a housing officer, so I'm the one ringing them to ask why a boiler's still not fixed after three weeks.
Darren: Ah. So you're the enemy, then.
Claire: Sort of, yeah. I've got a family at the moment with a toddler and no heating, and the contractor keeps sending someone out to top up the pressure and leave. It drives me mad.
Darren: Yeah, that's the cheap fix, that. Usually it's a leak or the expansion vessel. Topping it up just buys you a fortnight.
Claire: That's what I thought. Why do they keep doing it, then?
Darren: Erm, honestly? Those contracts are priced tight. The firm gets a fixed rate per call-out, so the bloke's got eight jobs that day and he does the quickest thing. Not saying it's right, but that's how it works.
Claire: That's really useful, actually. I can push them on the vessel. Do you do much housing association work?
Darren: Not really. Mostly private, homeowners. Better money, to be fair, and they don't argue the bill as much.
Claire: I bet. How do you price things? I always wonder whether quotes are, you know, fair.
Darren: Ha, depends who's asking. No, it's parts, labour, bit for the van. Everyone does it a bit different. I keep my customers happy, that's the main thing.
Claire: Fair enough. Is it busy at this time of year?
Darren: Winter's mad. January I was doing twelve-hour days. Knees are feeling it now.
Claire: I've got a dodgy knee from running, so I swim instead. Ladywell, early mornings, and the lido when it's warm enough.
Darren: Lido, in this country? Rather you than me.
Claire: It's freezing until about June, but it's lovely once you're in. Do you do anything to switch off?
Darren: Walk the dog, Bailey. Round the heath. Bit of golf, and Ipswich on telly. And a barbecue in the summer, I've got a new gas one I'm quite pleased with.
Claire: A gas engineer with a gas barbecue, that's very on brand.
Darren: Ha, never thought of it like that. You go away much?
Claire: Erm, trains, mostly. Ghent, Bruges, Lisbon last autumn. I try not to fly if I can help it.
Darren: Lisbon on a train? How long's that take?
Claire: Two days, sort of. With stops. I had a spreadsheet.
Darren: Blimey. I'll stick to the plane to Turkey, I think. Pool, all-inclusive, job done.
Claire: That's fair. I think we're nearly out of time.
Darren: Yeah, think so. Good luck with that boiler, Claire. Ask about the vessel.
Claire: I will. Thanks, Darren, that was genuinely helpful.

Claire: I'm good, thanks. I'm Claire. Erm, a bit thrown by that puzzle at the start, if I'm honest. How about you?
Nicola: Oh God, the puzzle. I sort of stared at it for ages and then just guessed. Anyway, I'm alright, thanks. Bit stiff today, the weather's been doing my joints in, but I'm fine. Where are you, then?
Claire: Catford, South East London. And you?
Nicola: St Helens. Between Liverpool and Wigan, if you've not heard of it. I've got to say, I was looking at your photo earlier and I was dying to have a proper nosy at your bookshelf.
Claire: My bookshelf! Oh, it's a mess, honestly. It's mostly Scandi crime and whatever my book group's made me read. We're doing, erm, a Jon Fosse at the moment, which is sort of hard going.
Nicola: Oh, I tried one of his. Library e-book. It's all one long sentence, isn't it? I had to keep stopping. I'm more of a historical fiction person, and poetry. Carol Ann Duffy, Simon Armitage.
Claire: Oh, I love Armitage. Do you get through a lot?
Nicola: Loads. It's sort of all I can do some days, to be honest. I'm off work long-term with rheumatoid arthritis, so... I'm not being miserable about it, it's just how it is. The library app's my best friend. Except there's a waiting list on the one I want now, I'm about fortieth.
Claire: Fortieth! That's brutal. What did you do before, if you don't mind me asking?
Nicola: No, not at all. I was a care assistant in a residential home for years, then a school kitchen. I loved the care work, you know. Sitting with people, hearing the same story about their wedding for the fifth time. I miss that, do you know what I mean?
Claire: Yeah, I do, actually. That's kind of the bit of my job I like best.
Nicola: What do you do?
Claire: I'm a housing officer, for a housing association. I've got a patch of about three hundred flats across Lewisham and Greenwich, so it's sign-ups, home visits, rent arrears, neighbour disputes. A lot of it's paperwork, but the visits are where you actually find out what's going on with people. Some days it's lovely, and some days it's, erm, damp and mould and a family of five in a one-bed, and you come home and you can't switch off.
Nicola: Oh, that's funny, I rent off a housing association. Two-bed, me and the two kids.
Claire: Oh, really? Are they any good? You can be honest, I won't take it personally.
Nicola: They're alright, actually. They took six weeks to fix the back door once, but they put the grab rails in quick when I asked. I think it depends who you get, doesn't it? If you get someone who rings you back, that's half of it.
Claire: That's exactly it. I'm a bit obsessive about ringing people back. If I say Thursday, I ring Thursday.
Nicola: See, you'd be one of the good ones.
Claire: I try. What else fills your days, besides the reading?
Nicola: Birds, mainly. I've got a nest box out the back and the blue tits are back in it, I'm made up. And I do little watercolours when my hands let me. I start loads and finish about one in five.
Claire: That's better than my pottery. I make mugs that come out a weird colour and give them to people who are too polite to say anything.
Nicola: I'd have one! Are those the ones on your top shelf?
Claire: Yeah, those are the survivors. The green one was meant to be blue.
Nicola: Ah, it's character, that. My Ellie's the creative one in our house now, she's fifteen. She's been doing TikTok recipes, made us a Thai green curry for tea last week and it was actually lovely.
Claire: Oh, good on her. I keep trying to do Ottolenghi for dinner and it takes me about three hours.
Nicola: Ellie'd have a go at that. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry.
Claire: No, not at all, this is nice. I think we've probably not got long left, have we?
Nicola: No, it goes quick, doesn't it? It's been lovely talking to you, Claire.
Claire: You too. Good luck with the waiting list.
calls.C0391:
Darren: Hello, there we go. Can you hear me alright?
Rasa: Yes, hello. I can hear you. I'm Rasa.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from, then?
Rasa: Leyton, East London. And you?
Darren: Kesgrave, just outside Ipswich. Suffolk.
Rasa: Ah, okay. I don't know it, sorry. I know Ipswich only from the train board.
Darren: Ha, that's most people, to be fair. It's alright, it's quiet. So what do you do, Rasa?
Rasa: I work in a bakery in Walthamstow. Part-time, Saturday morning and one day in the week. Saturday is crazy, queue out the door from eight o'clock.
Darren: I bet. What, all the sausage rolls?
Rasa: Sausage rolls, yeah, and the bread. Everybody wants sourdough now. I bring home what is left at the end, so we never buy bread, that's good. And you? I guessed from your photo maybe builder or plumber.
Darren: Not far off. Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Installs, servicing, breakdowns. Got me own business, one van, been doing it about fourteen years.
Rasa: Oh, really? Then I need you. My boiler, every winter it stops. The pressure goes down, and the landlord takes like two weeks to send someone.
Darren: Yeah, that's a classic, that. Pressure dropping, you've probably got a little leak somewhere or the expansion vessel's gone. Landlord's probably just getting the cheapest bloke round to top it up, you know.
Rasa: Yes! Exactly. The man comes, he does something for five minutes and goes. And then three weeks later, again.
Darren: Sounds about right. It's mad busy in the winter anyway. Everyone's boiler packs up the first cold week. I was doing twelve-hour days in January.
Rasa: Twelve hours, every day? You must be knackered.
Darren: Yeah, the knees aren't what they were, to be fair. I'm hoping to take on an apprentice in a year or two, so I can do more of the quoting and less lying on kitchen floors.
Rasa: That makes sense. My husband is electrician, he says same thing about his back.
Darren: Oh, is he? Self-employed?
Rasa: No, he works for a company, maintenance for buildings. This week he is in Stratford on a job. He likes it, regular money, you know.
Darren: Yeah, there's a lot to be said for that. Being your own boss sounds good till the van breaks down. Mine's been playing up, sensor fault, had it in the garage last week. Are you from London originally?
Rasa: No, I'm from Lithuania, from Šiauliai. I came in 2006. So, nearly twenty years now.
Darren: Twenty years, blimey. Do you get back much?
Rasa: Every summer. Two, three weeks with my mum and my sister. We fly from Stansted, Ryanair. My daughter, she is twelve, she loves it there because grandma spoils her.
Darren: Course she does. Mine were the same with my mum. We usually do Spain or Turkey, all-inclusive, pool, bit of sun. Did Florida once with the kids, that was something.
Rasa: Florida, wow. That's expensive, no?
Darren: Erm, yeah, you don't want to know. Worth it, though. Lithuania, that's basketball, isn't it? I remember something about that.
Rasa: Yes! Basketball is like religion there. I don't really follow, but when Lithuania plays in big tournament, my husband watches and I have to watch too. That's it, really.
Darren: Ha, same as me with Ipswich and my wife. She just sits there on her phone.
Rasa: Yeah, same. I make dinner and I hear him shouting from the other room.
Darren: Sounds like ours on a Saturday. Right, I reckon we're nearly out of time.
Rasa: Yeah, it's fast. Nice to talk to you, Darren.
Darren: You too, Rasa. Get your landlord to sort that vessel out.
calls.C0392:
Megan: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
Claire: Yes, hi! I can hear you fine. I'm Claire.
Megan: I'm Megan. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous, I always think I'm doing these wrong.
Claire: Oh, I think we all are. That puzzle at the start threw me completely.
Megan: Oh my God, same. I read the instructions twice and still wasn't sure. Erm, where are you based?
Claire: Catford, South East London. You?
Megan: Stockton-on-Tees. Norton, technically, if that makes sense. North East, but not Newcastle.
Claire: Not Newcastle, noted. I won't say Geordie.
Megan: Thank you! People always do. So what do you do?
Claire: I'm a housing officer for a housing association. I look after about three hundred flats, so it's home visits, rent arrears, repairs, people falling out with their neighbours. Quite a lot of listening, really. What about you? I guessed nursing from your photo, I don't know why.
Megan: Close! I'm doing diagnostic radiography at Teesside, second year. So X-rays, basically, and then CT and things later. I've got placements at James Cook and North Tees, so it's sort of half uni, half hospital.
Claire: Oh, that's interesting. Do you like the hospital side?
Megan: I do, yeah. I get dead anxious before placements, like I can't sleep the night before sometimes, but once I'm there it's fine. I'm good with the older patients, they're usually nervous as well, so we're nervous together. My shifts start at half seven, so I'm up at six, and the parking at James Cook is shocking, honestly.
Claire: Hospital parking, that's universal, isn't it? Was it always radiography for you?
Megan: Erm, no, not really. I started Biomedical Science at eighteen and left after the first year, it felt a bit too abstract. Then I worked in a pharmacy for nearly three years. So I'm kind of a bit behind, if that makes sense.
Claire: Behind? I don't think that's behind at all. I did my housing qualification part-time in my thirties, and half the people on it were career changers. Working in a pharmacy probably makes you better at the patient bit, you know?
Megan: Yeah, that's what my mam says. And the paperwork. I'm quite fussy about request forms because of the pharmacy.
Claire: That's a good thing to be fussy about. I'm the same with case notes. Colleagues tease me, but then they come and ask me what they wrote.
Megan: Ha, yeah. Is your job quite stressful, then?
Claire: Erm, sometimes, yeah. Damp and mould cases, families squashed into one-beds. You do take some of it home. I swim in the mornings, which helps clear my head.
Megan: I do parkrun, when I'm not on placement. Preston Park, Saturday mornings. I'm on week five of my running plan as well.
Claire: Week five, that's good going. I gave up running, dodgy knee. Do you live near the hospital?
Megan: No, I'm at home with my mam and stepdad and my little brother. He's sixteen and eats everything in the fridge. My mam's done mince and dumplings for tea tonight, so I'll have to be quick.
Claire: Mince and dumplings, that sounds lovely. My husband works evenings so I mostly cook dinner for one.
Megan: Oh, that's a shame. Is that a lot of cooking for one person?
Claire: Too much, usually. I make Ottolenghi things that take three hours and then eat them for four days.
Megan: Sorry, I'm just thinking, I don't even know what Ottolenghi is. Is that a person?
Claire: It is, yes, a chef. Lots of pomegranate. You're not missing much on a Tuesday.
Megan: I'll stick with my chicken and rice in a tub, I think.
Claire: Honestly, that sounds very sensible. I think we're nearly out of time.
Megan: Oh, already? It's been really nice, thank you.
Claire: You too, Megan. Good luck with placement.
calls.C0393:
Nicola: Hiya! Can you hear me, love?
Rasa: Yes, I hear you. Hello, I'm Rasa.
Nicola: Nicola. Nice to meet you. How are you doing today?
Rasa: I'm okay, thank you. Bit tired. And you?
Nicola: Oh, same, I'm always a bit tired, don't worry. Where are you?
Rasa: Leyton, East London.
Nicola: I'm St Helens, up near Liverpool. I'll be honest, when I saw your photo I thought, she looks like a busy mum like me. Nice tidy kitchen, mind. Mine's a tip.
Rasa: Ha, it's tidy only for the photo. I thought same about you, tired mum. How many kids?
Nicola: Two. Ellie's fifteen and Jake's twelve. You?
Rasa: One. Emilija, she is twelve. Year 8.
Nicola: Same as Jake! Are they driving you mad yet? Jake's football boots already don't fit him, I only bought them in September.
Rasa: Yes, the shoes. And the school, always they want money for something. Now is some project, we have to buy another thing. Every week another thing.
Nicola: Oh, tell me about it. And everything's gone up. I do most of mine at Aldi and the reduced shelf, and even that's dear now.
Rasa: Lidl for me. Prices are crazy, yeah. Do you work?
Nicola: Not at the minute, no. I've got rheumatoid arthritis, so I've been off sick about four years. I used to be a carer in a residential home. Ellie does a lot of the shopping now, bless her, and some of the cooking. She did a Thai green curry from TikTok last week and it was actually lovely.
Rasa: Oh, that's nice she helps. Thai curry, it's spicy, no?
Nicola: A bit, yeah. Are you not a spice person?
Rasa: No, not really. I'm Lithuanian, we eat potatoes, potatoes, more potatoes. At weekend I made cepelinai, it takes all afternoon.
Nicola: What's cepelinai, then? Sorry, have I said that right?
Rasa: Yes, close. It's like big potato dumpling, with meat inside, and you put sour cream and bacon on top. Shape like a zeppelin, that's why the name. My daughter loves it, my husband loves it, I'm knackered after.
Nicola: Oh, that sounds right up my street. We do scouse when it's cold, which is sort of the same idea, meat and potato and you're full till next week.
Rasa: Scouse is what?
Nicola: It's a stew, lamb or beef with potatoes and carrots, cooked for ages. Liverpool thing. You have it with red cabbage and bread. Do you cook every night?
Rasa: Most nights, yes. I make dinner, if I'm tired then pasta. I work in bakery, so we always have bread, I bring home what's left.
Nicola: Free bread! I'd be made up with that. Do you go back to Lithuania much?
Rasa: Every summer, two or three weeks. My mum is there alone, so I worry a bit. We speak on video every Sunday.
Nicola: Ah, that's nice you do that. My mum died two years ago and I still go to ring her sometimes, do you know what I mean? So keep doing your Sundays.
Rasa: Yes. I'm sorry about your mum.
Nicola: Thank you, love. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry. I think we're nearly done.
Rasa: Yeah, it was nice to talk to you, Nicola.
Nicola: You too, Rasa. Enjoy your cepelinai.
calls.C0394:
Darren: Hello, there we go. Can you hear me alright?
Megan: Yeah, I can hear you. Hiya, I'm Megan.
Darren: Darren. Nice to meet you, Megan. Where are you, then?
Megan: Stockton-on-Tees, in the North East. Well, Norton, which is just next to it. What about you?

Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, mostly. Run me own business, one van, been doing it about fourteen years now.
Megan: Oh, that's funny, I thought you'd be something like that. You reminded me of my stepdad in your photo. He's an electrician at one of the chemical plants on Teesport.
Darren: Ha, I'll take that. Proper job, that. Is he alright to live with?
Megan: He's lovely, yeah. Very calm. Him and my mam have been married eleven years.
Darren: Good for them. What about you, are you working?
Megan: I'm a student, second year of diagnostic radiography at Teesside. So I do X-rays, basically, and placements at the hospitals, James Cook and North Tees. It's kind of half lectures and half being on the wards, if that makes sense. I start at half seven on placement, so I'm up at six, and the A19 is a nightmare in the mornings. I was sat in traffic for ages yesterday.
Darren: Half seven's not too bad, to be fair. I'm usually out the door about then. You drive in, do you?
Megan: Yeah, I've got a little Corsa. Second-hand, but it does the job.
Darren: That's all you need. My lad Callum's learning to drive at the minute, seventeen. Lessons are costing a fortune, and the insurance quotes, don't get me started.
Megan: Oh, my brother's called Callum! He's sixteen though, so not driving yet, thank God. He just eats everything in the fridge.
Darren: Ha, sounds about right. Mine's the same. You go to the fridge for a bit of ham and it's gone.
Megan: Exactly that. Is it busy, your job? Like, all the time?
Darren: Winter's mad. First cold week, everyone's boiler packs up at once. I was doing twelve-hour days in January. Summer's quieter, that's when you do your installs. I did my heat pump ticket a couple of years back as well, 'cause that's where it's all heading, you know.
Megan: Oh right. Are heat pumps better, then? Sorry, I don't really know anything about them.
Darren: Erm, they can be. Depends on the house, really. Good insulation, they're great. Old draughty place, you're better off with a decent boiler. I tell people straight what'll work for them.
Megan: That's good. My stepdad says the same about his job, that people just want someone to tell them what to do.
Darren: That's half of it, yeah. Keep 'em happy. Do you like the hospital side?
Megan: I do. I get a bit nervous before placements, but I'm good with the older patients. They're usually more nervous than me, so I just talk them through it. I keep a little notebook in my tunic pocket for all the settings, 'cause I'm worried I'll forget something.
Darren: Sounds like you're doing it right to me. Better nervous than cocky.
Megan: Yeah, that's what my supervisor sort of said. Do you watch football? My stepdad has Boro on all the time.
Darren: Ipswich, yeah. They've done alright lately, been to Portman Road a few times. Good atmosphere.
Megan: I couldn't name more than about three Boro players, honestly. I just sit there with him.
Darren: Ha, that's my missus with Ipswich. Right, I think that's us about done.
Megan: Oh, is it? That went fast. It was nice talking to you, Darren.
Darren: You too, Megan. Good luck with the placements, yeah.
calls.C0395:
Nicola: Hiya! Can you hear me alright, love?
Darren: Yeah, loud and clear. Hello. I'm Darren.
Nicola: Darren! Oh, that's funny. My husband's called Darren. Well, sort of ex-husband. We're separated, never got round to the divorce.
Darren: Ha, hopefully I'm not putting you off, then.
Nicola: No, no, he's alright, we get on fine. I'm Nicola, anyway. Where are you?
Darren: Kesgrave, near Ipswich. Suffolk. You?
Nicola: St Helens, between Liverpool and Wigan. I'll be honest, I looked at your photo and thought, he looks like my dad or one of my brothers. Just a normal bloke who knows what he's doing.
Darren: I'll take that, to be fair. I said you reminded me of my wife, Karen, so we're even.
Nicola: Oh, bless you. What do you do, then?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Got my own business, one van, about fourteen years now.
Nicola: Ooh, I could do with you. Mine makes this horrible banging noise when the heating first comes on. The housing association sent someone and he said it was normal.
Darren: Banging? Could be air in the system, or a bit of sludge in the pipes. It's not dangerous usually, but it's not normal either. I'd get them back out, if I'm honest.
Nicola: See, I knew it. I'll ring them. Do you like it, the job?
Darren: Yeah, I do. It's good money if you put the hours in. Winter's mad, everyone's boiler packs up the first cold week. My knees don't thank me, mind.
Nicola: Oh, I know all about knees. I've got rheumatoid arthritis, so I've been off work about four years now. I was a carer in a residential home before that. I miss it, you know, the people.
Darren: That's a shame. That's a proper job, caring. Harder than mine, probably.
Nicola: Ah, I don't know about that. You're the one lying on kitchen floors.
Darren: Ha, true. I'm hoping to get an apprentice in, so I can do more quoting and less crawling about.
Nicola: That's sensible. My dad worked at the glassworks his whole life and his back was knackered by fifty. So you look after yourself.
Darren: Yeah, my dad was a lorry driver, same sort of thing. Wrecked by the end. I've done a bit better than him, I think. Bigger house, my own van, you know. That means something.
Nicola: Course it does. He'd be proud of you, I bet. Was he an Ipswich fan?
Darren: Oh yeah, that's where I got it from. Do you follow anything?
Nicola: Rugby league, half-heartedly. Saints, 'cause of my dad. I'll have the Challenge Cup final on, but I couldn't tell you the league table.
Darren: That's like my missus with the football. She sits there on her phone the whole match.
Nicola: Ha, that'd be me. I'd have a book on my knee. How many kids have you got?
Darren: Two. Jess is twenty-one, moved to Colchester with her boyfriend last year. And Callum's seventeen, learning to drive. Costing me a fortune.
Nicola: Oh, do you miss your Jess?
Darren: Erm, yeah. More than I'd tell her, to be fair. She's round most Sundays, though, for a roast.
Nicola: Ah, that's lovely. Mine are fifteen and twelve, so I've got all that to come. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry.
Darren: No, you're alright. I think that's us nearly done, actually.
Nicola: Already? It's been lovely talking to you, Darren.
Darren: You too, Nicola. Get that boiler looked at, yeah.
calls.C0396:
Megan: Hiya, can you hear me okay?
Nicola: Yeah, I can hear you, love. Hiya, I'm Nicola.
Megan: I'm Megan. Sorry, I always say that at the start, like the internet's going to go.
Nicola: Ah, you're fine. How are you doing? Have they worn you out yet?
Megan: A bit, yeah. I'm okay, though. Erm, I'm in Stockton, Norton really. Where are you?
Nicola: St Helens, up by Liverpool. I'll be honest, when I saw your photo I thought, she looks like me when I was starting out in care. Tired but capable.
Megan: Oh, that's really nice. I'm not in care, but sort of near it. I'm doing radiography, second year, so X-rays. And I thought you looked really easy to talk to. You reminded me a bit of my nanna, actually.
Nicola: Your nanna! Oh, I'll take that, love, even if it makes me feel ancient.
Megan: Sorry, I meant it in a nice way! She's lovely. I do jigsaws with her most Sundays.
Nicola: No, I know you did, I'm only teasing. Radiography, though. I've had more X-rays than hot dinners, me. I've got rheumatoid arthritis, so it's hands, feet, chest, the lot.
Megan: Oh no. Do you find it alright, having them done?
Nicola: Mostly, yeah. The ones I remember are the radiographers who don't rush you. When your hands are bad and someone's trying to get your fingers flat on the plate, and they just say, take your time, there's no hurry. That makes the whole day better, do you know what I mean?
Megan: Yeah. That's kind of what I worry about, getting it wrong with someone like that. I'm good with older patients, I think, but I check everything about five times.
Nicola: Better that than not checking. I did care work for years, and the ones who worried were always the good ones.
Megan: That's sort of what my supervisor says. Did you like care work?
Nicola: I loved it. Sitting with people, listening. I'm off sick now, about four years. I miss it.
Megan: I bet. Erm, sorry, I'm just thinking what to ask. What do you do in the day, then?
Nicola: Read, mostly. Watch the birds. I do little watercolours when my hands let me. And telly, I watch these Danish crime dramas with subtitles.
Megan: I couldn't do subtitles, I'd be on my phone and miss it. I'm Bake Off and Gogglebox. And Friends repeats, honestly.
Nicola: Oh, Bake Off's lovely. My Ellie's mad on cooking now, she's fifteen. TikTok recipes.
Megan: My brother's sixteen and he just eats. My mam made mince and dumplings for tea and he'd had half of it before I got in.
Nicola: Mince and dumplings! We call it tea up here too. My treat's a chip barm.
Megan: Mine's a parmo on a Friday. I share it with my brother though, I can't finish a whole one.
Nicola: What's a parmo, love?
Megan: Oh, it's a Teesside thing. Breaded chicken with béchamel sauce and cheese on top, with chips. It's massive.
Nicola: Oh, that sounds dangerous. I'd have a go at that.
Megan: You should, if you're ever up. Is that time already?
Nicola: I think so. It's been lovely, Megan. Give your nanna my best.
Megan: I will. Thank you, it was really nice talking to you.
calls.C0397:
Claire: Hello, hi. Can you hear me?
Darren: Yeah, hello. I'm Darren.
Claire: Claire. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from?
Darren: Kesgrave, near Ipswich. You?
Claire: Catford, South East London. What do you do, Darren?
Darren: Gas engineer. Boilers, heating. Self-employed, one van, about fourteen years.
Claire: Oh, I'll be honest, I guessed something like that. You reminded me of some of the contractors I work with.
Darren: Ha, is that good or bad?
Claire: Mostly good. Depends on the contractor. I'm a housing officer, so I'm the one ringing them to ask why a boiler's still not fixed after three weeks.
Darren: Ah. So you're the enemy, then.
Claire: Sort of, yeah. I've got a family at the moment with a toddler and no heating, and the contractor keeps sending someone out to top up the pressure and leave. It drives me mad.
Darren: Yeah, that's the cheap fix, that. Usually it's a leak or the expansion vessel. Topping it up just buys you a fortnight.
Claire: That's what I thought. Why do they keep doing it, then?
Darren: Erm, honestly? Those contracts are priced tight. The firm gets a fixed rate per call-out, so the bloke's got eight jobs that day and he does the quickest thing. Not saying it's right, but that's how it works.
Claire: That's really useful, actually. I can push them on the vessel. Do you do much housing association work?
Darren: Not really. Mostly private, homeowners. Better money, to be fair, and they don't argue the bill as much.
Claire: I bet. How do you price things? I always wonder whether quotes are, you know, fair.
Darren: Ha, depends who's asking. No, it's parts, labour, bit for the van. Everyone does it a bit different. I keep my customers happy, that's the main thing.
Claire: Fair enough. Is it busy at this time of year?
Darren: Winter's mad. January I was doing twelve-hour days. Knees are feeling it now.
Claire: I've got a dodgy knee from running, so I swim instead. Ladywell, early mornings, and the lido when it's warm enough.
Darren: Lido, in this country? Rather you than me.
Claire: It's freezing until about June, but it's lovely once you're in. Do you do anything to switch off?
Darren: Walk the dog, Bailey. Round the heath. Bit of golf, and Ipswich on telly. And a barbecue in the summer, I've got a new gas one I'm quite pleased with.
Claire: A gas engineer with a gas barbecue, that's very on brand.
Darren: Ha, never thought of it like that. You go away much?
Claire: Erm, trains, mostly. Ghent, Bruges, Lisbon last autumn. I try not to fly if I can help it.
Darren: Lisbon on a train? How long's that take?
Claire: Two days, sort of. With stops. I had a spreadsheet.
Darren: Blimey. I'll stick to the plane to Turkey, I think. Pool, all-inclusive, job done.
Claire: That's fair. I think we're nearly out of time.
Darren: Yeah, think so. Good luck with that boiler, Claire. Ask about the vessel.
Claire: I will. Thanks, Darren, that was genuinely helpful.
